paragraphs: Qayma lan: kol hayyotze min hattame – tame. lepikak chaleb behema vechayya temea o terepa, asur kibsarah; vehu haddin tzirah, name asur kibsarah. lepikak otam sheshshotim chaleb haaton lirpua, en lishtot ella becholi shel sakkana, vegam tzarik sheyyomar ken rope mumcheh; abal nashim sheosin atzman laropein, veomerim lebaal hacholi lishtot chaleb attun veyitrappe - asur lo lismok al dibrehem. veayyen machaziq beraka, siman p" ot '.

clarification.explanation: The rule is "whatever emerges from the impure is impure" — that is, anything emerging from the body of an impure domestic or wild animal, or from a treifah animal, has the same law as its meat, and is therefore forbidden. Accordingly, the milk of an impure or treifah animal is likewise forbidden, as are its secretions. From this, one who wishes to drink donkey's milk for medicinal purposes — a donkey being an impure animal — may do so only for a life-threatening illness, and only on the instruction of a genuine, qualified physician. But if amateur women posing as doctors advise someone to drink donkey's milk, he may not rely on their words, since the permission depends on reliable medical judgment, not folk advice.
takeaways: The milk or secretions of an impure/treifah animal are forbidden like its meat.
Donkey's milk for medicine is permitted only for a life-threatening illness, on the instruction of a genuine, qualified physician.
One may not rely on advice from people who are not licensed physicians regarding such a leniency.

paragraphs: Me-raglayim shel behema vechayya temea o terepa, asurin kibsarah. veyesh mi shemmattir beme-raglayim, mippene sheen bain miggupah, ella mimmah shehiknisa legupah; chutz min me-raglayim shel chamor shehem asurim mippene shehem akurim vedomin lechalab dedino kebasar. al-ken becholeh sheen bo sakkana, yesh lismok al hammattirin beme-raglayim shel behema vechayya chutz mechamur; vetzarik gam ken sheyyomar rope mumcheh; vegam bitnay shei epshar laasot lo repua bedabar acher. veim kol zeh, hannizhar, tabo alayv beraka, ki beemet yesh lachush lisbarat haoserin bekol me-raglayim, asher maran za"l satam kevatayhu; abal me-raglayim shel chamor, asur middina becholeh sheen bo sakkana, mishshum degam hammattirin beme-raglayim, modim leesor beshel chamor. v"g demaran za"l sebira lah dehammattirin beme-raglayim, mattirin gam beshel chamor - en ken daat happoseqim, disbira lah dehammattirin modo leesor beshel chamor. veayyen sha"k uperi chadash ushear acharonim.

clarification.explanation: The urine of an impure or treifah domestic or wild animal is likewise forbidden like its meat. There is a lenient opinion regarding urine in general, on the grounds that it does not "emerge from the body itself" exactly, but rather is what the animal drank, entered its body, and exited — making it less similar to the flesh itself. But an exception is the urine of a donkey, which is thick and resembles milk (whose law is like meat), and is therefore forbidden even according to the lenient view. The practical conclusion: for a patient who is not dangerously ill, one may rely on the lenient view regarding the urine of other animals (not a donkey), provided a qualified physician says it is necessary and there is no alternative medicine. Nevertheless, one who is stringent with himself and avoids this too is proper and blessed, since there is room for concern for the forbidding view, which Maran also ruled. But donkey's urine is entirely forbidden even for a non-dangerously ill patient, since all opinions agree to forbid it, even though some thought Maran permits it — this is not the view of most authorities.
takeaways: The urine of an impure/treifah animal is forbidden like its meat.
Donkey's urine is always forbidden, even for a non-dangerously ill patient.
Other animals' urine (not donkey) may be lenient for a non-dangerously ill patient only with a qualified physician's approval and no alternative medicine, though being stringent is praiseworthy.

paragraphs: Im hachamor hishtin veqelach meat letok haqqeara sheyyesh bah mashqeh o tabshil lach venitareb, tzarik shishshim keneged me-raglayim; veim qelach al maakol yabesh, yedichennu vishapshepennu heteb vedayyo. vekol zeh beme-raglayim shel chamor, abal shel shear behema vechayya - im napelu letok mashqeh o tabshil lach venitarebu veen shishshim lebattelam, muttar lehosip alehem lebattelam, veen lachush mishshum deen mebattelin issur lekattechilla, mishshum deikka poseqim mattirim beme-raglayim shel behemot chutz mechamur; veim qlch al maakol yabesh, tzarik lahadicho uleshapshepo heteb.

clarification.explanation: If donkey's urine dripped into a cooked dish or liquid beverage and mixed in, the dish must contain sixty times the urine's volume to be permitted; and if it fell on dry food, thorough rinsing and scrubbing suffices. This applies specifically to donkey's urine, which is more severe. But for the urine of other domestic and wild animals (not a donkey), if it fell into a liquid beverage or dish and there is not sixty times its volume to nullify it — it is even permitted to add more of the dish to complete the sixty, and there is no problem of "deliberately nullifying a prohibition," since there are already authorities who permit the urine of animals (other than a donkey) even without nullification. And if it fell on dry food — here too, thorough rinsing and scrubbing suffices.
takeaways: Donkey's urine that fell into a liquid requires sixty times its volume for nullification; on dry food, rinsing and scrubbing suffice.
Other animals' urine (not donkey) that fell into a liquid without sixty times its volume — one may add more of the dish to nullify it.
The distinction between a donkey and other animals affects the severity of the law.

paragraphs: Hannolad min hatterepa, muttar; v"g deqayma lan: ubbar yerek immo hu, mikkol maqom leinyan terepot shane, kevan deen issura shel haem ella raq mishshum chayyut, ditrepa enah chayya, veubbar zeh chay hu veen chayyuto taluy bachayyot haem; mihu, im nidresa haem beod havvalad betokah - asur havvalad mesappeqa, deepshar tippat haeres shel hadderisa yazziq gam lavvalad; abal im yatza havvalad vachay y"b chodesh, az muttar. veim shachatu oto tok y"b chodesh, asur missapeq. vekol zeh benidresa lepanenu keneged hechalal, deaz chosheshin lavvalad, abal im nidresa betzavvarah o beragleha vekayyotze, havvalad muttar, devadday en tippat haeres shel hadderisa maggaat lavvalad. veim niknas haddores laddir, veaach"k nimtza tzipporen tachub beachat mehem vehaober betziddah, velo noda im ad shello nidresa yaleda, o achar shennidresa yaleda - havvalad asur missapeq.

clarification.explanation: An offspring born from a mother who is treifah (an animal with a defect causing death within a short time) is permitted for eating. This seemingly presents a difficulty, since halacha states "a fetus is the thigh of its mother" (the fetus is considered part of the mother's body), and it would seem it should therefore be forbidden like her. But regarding the laws of treifah this is different: the mother's prohibition of treifah stems only from her not being "alive" (lacking vitality), whereas the offspring itself is alive, and its vitality does not depend on its mother's vitality. However, if the mother was mauled (wounded by a predator) while pregnant, the offspring is forbidden out of doubt, since there is concern that poison from the wound may have permeated to it as well. If the offspring emerged and lived twelve months, this is a sign it is healthy and permitted; if slaughtered within the twelve months — it is forbidden out of doubt. And all this applies specifically when the wound was against the body cavity (the abdomen/chest area); if the wound was in the neck or legs, the offspring is certainly permitted, since it is clear the poison did not reach it. If it is not known exactly when the offspring was born relative to the wound — it is forbidden out of doubt.
takeaways: An offspring from a treifah mother is permitted, since its vitality does not depend on the mother's.
If the mother was mauled while the offspring was in her womb against the body cavity — the offspring is forbidden out of doubt until it lives 12 months.
A wound in the neck/legs does not affect the offspring's permitted status.

paragraphs: Besar haadam asur leakelo min hattora, v"g deyesh omerim deissuro midderabbanan veim peresh muttar - haiqqar kedibre haoserim bekol gavna; mihu, or haadam eno asur ella midderabbanan. veayyen sipte daat, siman "t, seip qatan g'. vetzarik lizzaher shello liqlop o lachtok or haadam beshinnayv, pen yishshaer qetzat ben shinnayv o bepiv; vegam yesh lachush sheyyachtok qetzat min habbasar gam-ken. umah shennahagu hannashim libloa arelat hazzekarim shechotekim beet hammila kede sheyyolidu zekarim - issur chamur hu zeh, ukemo shekkatab machaziq beraka, ot b', beshem hrshb"sh za"l.

clarification.explanation: Human flesh is Torah-forbidden for eating. There is an opinion that the prohibition is only rabbinic, and that if the flesh is separated from the body (for example, an amputated limb) it is entirely permitted — but the practical halacha follows the stricter view, that the prohibition applies in every case. By contrast, human skin is forbidden only rabbinically (a lighter prohibition). One must therefore be very careful not to peel or cut human skin with the teeth, since there is concern that a bit might remain between the teeth or in the mouth, and also concern one might accidentally cut a bit of the flesh itself. Likewise, the custom that existed among certain women of swallowing the foreskin cut off at a circumcision, out of a belief this would cause them to bear male children, is a severe prohibition and should not be practiced.
takeaways: Human flesh is Torah-forbidden; human skin is only rabbinically forbidden.
One must be careful not to peel or cut human skin with the teeth.
The custom of swallowing a foreskin at a circumcision is a severe prohibition to be avoided.

paragraphs: H"mumayya" (gupat adam chanuta) shehu besar haadam, muttar lirpua apillu lecholeh sheen bo sakkana, deapra bealema hi. ayyen "erek- hashshulchan" beshem haradba"z za"l. veasur laasot segulla lecholeh, leashshen atzmo beshen met goy, deap al gab derecha lav milleta hi, mikkol maqom hanaat repua haveya hanaa veasur. v"g deyesh meqillin bemet goy, disbira lehu davqa met yisrael asur bahanaa - haiqqar kemo shekkatab mera"n za"l beyoreh dea, siman shm"t, dela shena ben goy leyisrael; veayyen "shiyyure-beraka" besiman shm"t.

clarification.explanation: "Mummia" — an embalmed corpse, which is essentially human flesh — is permitted for medicinal use, even for a non-dangerously ill patient, since it is already considered a kind of "dust" rather than actual flesh. By contrast, it is forbidden to practice the remedy of self-smoking using a dead gentile's tooth, since although the smoking itself (the scent) is not considered significant benefit, here it concerns the benefit of healing, and any healing benefit from a forbidden object is forbidden. There is a lenient opinion holding that only the body of a deceased Jew is forbidden for benefit, while the body of a deceased gentile is permitted — but the practical halacha, as Maran ruled, is that there is no difference between a gentile and a Jew, and both are forbidden for benefit.
takeaways: Mummified remains are permitted for medicine even for a non-dangerously ill patient, since considered dust.
Smoking with a dead gentile's tooth as a remedy is forbidden, since this is healing benefit.
There is no difference between a deceased Jew and a deceased gentile — both are forbidden for benefit.

paragraphs: Apillu lamman deamar besar adam asur min hattora, apillu hake, me-raglayim deadam muttarin ledibre hakkol, mippene shehem kammayim, veeno mitmatztze miggupo; umikkol maqom lekattechilla asurim mishshum "bal teshaqqetzu". velirpua bealema apillu choli meat sheen bo sakkana, shari, dekol sheoseh lirpua lo shayyak "bal teshaqqetzu"; veken hu haddin leezeh sibba kol dehu, shari vekannizkar bipri chadash. veim hishtin tinoq liqdera sheeno nikkar, muttar vekannizkar besipte daat. veayyen machaziq beraka ushear acharonim. veken im netano leechad me raglayim shello middato, en bazeh mishshum shiqqutz. veayyen "kareti", seip qatan b'. upoh irenu bagdad y" nohagin dekol mi sheyyecheleh becholi sheqqorin "chatzba" (chatzabta), mashqin oto achar sheyyitrappe meat me-raglayim shello middato, dehannashim omerot, im lo yashquhu, yihyeh serachon bepiv kol yamayv; ak haropeim en modim bazeh, veomerim shebbeare eroppa en mashqin, veim kol zeh en serachon bepihem. vehannashim omerot: en mishsham reaya, ki teba vaavir hammeqomot eno shaveh; al-ken osim kirtzonam. umeachar derob haqqarob lekol decholi zeh hu eno ella biqtannim en anachnu mochin beyadam; abal im nizdammen gadol shechala bazeh, vadday nakon sheyyizdarez lishmor atzmo mizzeh, shello yarimu lehashqoto.

clarification.explanation: Even according to the stricter view holding that human flesh is Torah-forbidden, human urine is entirely permitted according to all opinions, since it resembles water and is not considered to emerge from the body itself like flesh. Nevertheless, as the primary practice there is a prohibition of "you shall not make yourselves detestable," but for medicinal purposes — even for a mild, non-life-threatening illness — it is permitted, since anything done for healing is not included at all in "you shall not make yourselves detestable." It is likewise permitted for any other purpose. If an infant urinated into a cooking pot without anyone noticing, the food is permitted. Likewise, if someone was given urine without his knowledge, there is no issue of detestability here. In Baghdad it was customary for a child who fell ill with measles to be given a little urine to drink after recovering somewhat, believing that otherwise he would have bad breath for life — although doctors disagreed with this and showed that in Europe this is not practiced and yet there is no bad breath. Since most patients with this illness are young children, those who follow this practice are not protested against, but if an adult falls ill with this disease, it is proper for him to be careful and not allow himself to be tricked into drinking it.
takeaways: Human urine is permitted by strict law, though as the primary practice forbidden under "you shall not make yourselves detestable" except for a purpose (medicine, etc.).
For medicine, even a mild illness, it is entirely permitted, and likewise if done without knowledge or intent.
The Baghdad custom of giving urine to children with measles is not protested, but an adult should be careful not to be tricked into it.

paragraphs: Me-raglayim shel behema vechayya hattehorim, dinan keme-raglayim shel adam, d"g dehem muttarim hemma - asurim mishshum "bal teshaqqetzu"; vekol mah shekkatabnu beme-raglayim shel adam, hu haddin kan.

clarification.explanation: The urine of a pure domestic or wild animal has the same law as human urine: permitted by strict law, but forbidden as the primary practice under "you shall not make yourselves detestable." Everything stated in the previous halacha regarding human urine (permitted for medicine, for a purpose, etc.) applies here in the same way.
takeaways: The urine of a pure animal is permitted by law, forbidden as the primary practice under "you shall not make yourselves detestable."
The same laws as human urine apply — permitted for medicine and for a purpose.

paragraphs: Cheleb shel ishah muttar lekattechilla kemo shekkatub baggemara (ketubbot s, ), daapillu mitzvat perush en bo. bammeh debarim amurim? keshepperesh mimmenna letok hakkeli o letok hayyad, vaapillu letok hayyad shel haishsha atzmah; abal lehaniq gadol middaddeha, o apillu lachalob letok piv, hare zeh keyoneq min hashsheretz veasur middibre soperim, deate leichallope linoq gam mibbehema temea. veim abar, makkin oto makkat mardut. vaapillu lecholeh, kol sheen bo sakkana, asur. velaken, mah shellipamim haddad shel haishsha yesh bo ezeh makka, veenah meniqa et benah mimmennu, umebiim ishah acheret shettinaq hechalab middaddeha vetiplot - asur mishshum marit haayin, deroin otah yoneqet, vegam i epshar shello yikkanes letok piha.

clarification.explanation: A woman's milk is entirely permitted as the primary practice, as stated in the Gemara, and there is not even a measure of piety in avoiding it. This applies specifically when the milk is expressed into a vessel or into a hand (even the woman's own hand) and drunk that way. But if an adult person nurses directly from the breast, or even if milk is expressed directly into the mouth — this is considered like nursing from a creeping creature, and is rabbinically forbidden, out of concern that people might come to substitute and also nurse from an impure animal. One who transgresses this is given lashes of rebellion (a rabbinic penalty). Even for a non-dangerously ill patient — it is forbidden. Therefore, the custom that when a woman has a wound on her breast and cannot nurse her son directly, another woman is brought to nurse from the breast and then expel the milk to the infant — is forbidden, both due to appearance (it looks as though she is nursing an adult) and because it is practically impossible for a bit of milk not to enter the nursing woman's own mouth.
takeaways: A woman's milk expressed into a vessel or hand is entirely permitted as the primary practice.
Direct nursing of an adult from the breast, or expressing directly into the mouth, is rabbinically forbidden.
The custom of bringing another woman to nurse and expel milk to the infant is forbidden, also due to appearance.

paragraphs: Hattinoq yoneq ad sop arba shanim – lebari, vechamesh – lekachush. bammeh debarim amurim? keshello gemaluhu, abal im perash, dehaynu sheggemaluhu shelosha yamim meet leet achar esrim vearbaa chodesh, hare zeh asur lehachaziro; vehu shepperesh mittok buryo, abal im lo perash ella mittok choli sheeno yakol linoq uperash - yekolim lehachaziro veyakol linoq ad tashlum arba vechamesh shanim; mishshum dekol shepperesh mittok choli, have keillu lo perash kelal. veha deamerinan: im peresh g' yamim meet leet achar k"d chodesh mittok buryo deasur lehachaziro, haynu davqa shepperesh legamre, deeno shoteh chalab od kelal, abal im lo perash ella raq meimmo, veyoneq hu meishah acheret, yekola immo leheniqu apillu shepperesh mimmenna kamma yamim, ukemo shekkatab b"minchat-yaaqob" za"l, upashut.

clarification.explanation: An infant nurses milk until age four if healthy, and five if weak. This applies as long as he has not been weaned. But if he was weaned — that is, nursing was entirely stopped for three consecutive days after twenty-four months of age — it is forbidden to return him to nursing, provided the weaning was entirely voluntary and not due to compulsion. If the interruption was the result of an illness preventing him from nursing rather than a choice, he may be returned to nursing up to age four/five, since an interruption due to illness is considered as though he never stopped at all. Likewise, if the infant merely stopped nursing from his biological mother but continues nursing from another woman, his mother can still return to nursing him even after several days passed without nursing from her.
takeaways: Nursing is permitted until age 4 (healthy) or 5 (weak), as long as not entirely weaned.
Voluntary weaning of 3 days after 24 months forbids returning to nursing.
An interruption due to illness, or continued nursing from another woman, is not considered forbidding weaning.

paragraphs: Im perash mittok buryo g' yamim meet leet achar k"d chodesh, vechala choli sheyyesh bo sakkana, vehaya tzorek bachazarato - muttar lehachaziro; veachar shettistalleq hassakkana tzarik lehaprisho miyyad vekannizkar baacharonim. veyesh mattirin lehachaziro apillu im hu choleh sheen bo sakkana; veyesh lismok bazeh al hammeqillin beheka deikka tzorek harbeh bazeh, kevan dehu issur derabbanan.

clarification.explanation: If an infant was entirely and voluntarily weaned for three consecutive days after twenty-four months of age (and by the previous halacha it is forbidden to return him to nursing), but afterward fell ill with a life-threatening illness and there was a genuine medical need to return him to nursing — it is permitted to return him. Once the danger passes, he must be separated from nursing again immediately. There is a more lenient opinion permitting a return to nursing even for a non-life-threatening illness, and one may rely on this view when there is great need, since overall the prohibition is only rabbinic (not Torah-level), and therefore there is more room for leniency in a case of need.
takeaways: In a life-threatening situation, it is permitted to return to nursing even after complete weaning, separating him again immediately once the danger passes.
For a non-dangerous illness, with great need, one may rely on the lenient view, since the prohibition is only rabbinic.

paragraphs: Im peresh betok k"d chodesh venitabbera hashshana - nitabbera lattinoq, veyakol linoq ad sop k"h chodesh; veayyen mishbetzot zahab, seip qatan y"; abal im perash mittok buryo betok chodesh haibbur g' yamim meet leet: kegon shennolad br"ch nisan, venishlemu k"d chodashim baadar hashsheni, vehu peresh g' yamim meet leet baadar sheni shehu chodesh haesrim vachamishsha yesh lehachmir veasur lehachaziro, dehave keperesh leachar k"d chodesh, vekannizkar bemabtzot zahab ushear acharonim za"l.

clarification.explanation: If the infant was weaned within the twenty-four-month period (before reaching that age), and that year was a leap year (a Hebrew leap year with an extra month of Adar) — the period is "extended" for the infant as well, meaning he may nurse until the completion of twenty-five months. But if the complete weaning (three consecutive days) fell within the leap month itself (for example, an infant born at the start of Nissan, whose twenty-fourth month falls in the second Adar, and the weaning occurred in that second Adar, which is actually the twenty-fifth month) — one should be stringent, since this is considered as though he was weaned after twenty-four months, and it is therefore forbidden to return him to nursing.
takeaways: In a leap year, the determining weaning age extends to twenty-five months.
If the weaning itself occurred within the leap month (second Adar), it has the law of weaning after 24 months, and returning to nursing is forbidden.

paragraphs: Mah sheomerim haolam: kol mah sheyyemaatu lavvalad biniqa, yihyeh havvalad yoter mukshar lattora, veal-ken gomelim oto achar shana o pachot mizzeh - taut hu beyadam, veissura ikka ligmol oto qodem k"d chodesh, im lo mechamat ibbur shennitabbera immo o sibba acheret hekrechit, vekannizkar b"pitche-teshuba" beshem "adone-paz", yeuyyan sham. vegam al pi hassod sheggilla rabbenu haari"y za"l, yesh lattinoq linoq k"d chodesh; umeporash hattaam b"tz-chayyim", shaar rp"ch, pereq z', yeuyyan sham. al-ken vadday lo yapeh osin lidchot et hashshaa, lehaqdim qodem k"d chodesh; ukebar neemar: "im tairu veim teoreru et haahaba ad shettechpatz". vehashshem yitbarek berachamayv harabbim yekapper baadenu, veyashub lanu et niddachenu, yiru enenu veyismach libbenu, baagala ubizman qarib amen ken yehi ratzon.

Veda delipamim yimtza hattinoq holek beraglayv achar shemona chodashim, veyimtza sheeno holek ella ad achar k"d chodesh - lekol zeh yesh taam "p hassod, umeporash b"tz-chayyim" sham, yeuyyan sham. laken im yireh adam sheachar hattinoq laleket, hinneh im lo aberu k"d chodashim al yidag al zeh, sheyyesh taam bazeh.

clarification.explanation: There is a folk belief that the less an infant nurses, the more capable he will be for Torah study, and therefore some were accustomed to wean infants early, after a year or less — but this is a mistake, and there is a prohibition against weaning an infant before twenty-four months, unless there is a compelling reason such as a leap year or a similar need. Also according to the mystical secret revealed by the holy Arizal, an infant should nurse specifically twenty-four months, the reason for which is explained in the book "Etz Chaim." Therefore it is not proper to rush or force the timing. One should add a prayer that the Holy One, blessed be He, will again have mercy on us and return our scattered ones. Likewise, there is a difference among infants regarding when they begin to walk — some walk already after eight months, and some only after twenty-four months — and this too has a reason according to the mystical secret explained in that same place in "Etz Chaim." Therefore one who sees that his infant is delayed in walking, if twenty-four months have not yet passed, need not worry, since there is an inner reason for this.
takeaways: It is forbidden to wean an infant before 24 months, even out of belief it will aid Torah study.
According to the mystical secret (the Arizal), 24 months of nursing is the proper measure, and the timing should not be rushed.
A delay in walking up to age 24 months is likewise no cause for concern — there is an inner reason for it.

paragraphs: Chaleb nakerit, ap al pi demin haddin dino kachaleb yisreelit, im kol zeh, im tzarik letinoq meneqet, yishtaddelu meod shello lahaniqo min hannakerit, mippene dachaleb nakerit metamtem halleb beyirat shamayim, umolid bo teba ra veakzariyyut; v"p shezzot hannakerit yoshebet bebet yisrael veokelet maakalim shel hetter bilbad - shomer napsho yirchaq mimmenna velo yitten et beno lah leheniqu; abal heka dei epshar beyisreelit beshum open, shari, dehave sakkana; veayyen mishbetzot zahab v"shiyyure-beraka". vaapillu meneqet yisreelit, im tokal bizman yeniqa debarim raim, kegon sheyyesh lah choli sheyyesh bo sakkana, veamar harope shettishteh cheleb attun vekayyotze lirpua, az chalabah yazziq lattinoq hezzeq nepashay; veken tizzaher shello tokal mocha veleb vekabed bizman hayyeniqa; veken hattinoq atzmo "p shehu qatan harbeh, lo yenichuhu leekol debarim asurim.

clarification.explanation: Technically, the milk of a gentile woman has the same law as the milk of a Jewish woman. Nevertheless, if there is a need to bring the infant a wet nurse, great effort should be made not to have him nurse specifically from a gentile, since a gentile's milk badly affects the infant — it dulls the heart's fear of Heaven and instills within him a bad and cruel nature. This is true even if the gentile woman lives in a Jewish home and eats only kosher food — one should still keep away from giving her the infant to nurse, due to the spiritual effect of her simply being a gentile. But if there is truly no other option (a situation of life-threatening danger), it is permitted. Likewise, even if the wet nurse herself is Jewish, but ate harmful things while nursing — for example, if she is dangerously ill and a doctor instructed her to drink donkey's milk for medicine — her milk could cause spiritual harm to the infant. Therefore the wet nurse must also be careful not to eat brain, heart, and liver during the nursing period. Likewise, even the infant himself, though very young, should not be allowed to eat forbidden foods.
takeaways: Although a gentile's milk is technically permitted, one should avoid her as a wet nurse due to spiritual effect, except in a life-threatening situation.
A Jewish wet nurse must be careful not to eat brain, heart, liver, or harmful medicines during nursing.
Even a very young infant should not be fed forbidden foods.

paragraphs: Debash-deborim shemmartichin oto beod gupe haddeborim meorabin bo, "g dehave noten taam lipgam - tzerikin lizzaher lekattechilla shello yechammemu oto beod haddeborim bo chom shehayyad soledet bo, ubediabad shari; veayyen "bet-lechem-yeuddeh" vesipte daat. vetzarik lehazhir haam bidbash-temarim, o shel sukkar shennapal bo nemalim vehu ab shei epshar lesanneno bilti chimmum kede sheyyihyeh nipshar - tzarik sheyyizzaharu lekattechilla shello yechammemuhu chom shehayyad soledet bo. gam tzarik lehazhiram sheim rau shennapal nemalim bidbash o shear mashqeh, sheyyesanneno oto miyyad, velo yishhu bo hannemalim g' yamim, kede shello yihyeh kabush; veayyen sipte daat, seip qatan k"z. ak bidbash-deborim i epshar lizzaher bazeh lekattechilla, yaan ki zeh mebiim oto mimmaqom rachoq, kebar nikbash kamma yamim beodo beyad haggoyim.

clarification.explanation: Bee honey boiled while the bees' bodies are still mixed into it — although by the rule of "imparting a spoiling taste" (that is, the bees only spoil the taste and are not considered a significant forbidden mixture) this is permitted — one should nevertheless, as the primary practice, be careful not to heat the honey to a heat that would burn a hand while the bees are still in it; but if this was already done, it is permitted after the fact. Likewise, date honey or sugar honey into which ants have fallen, which is too thick to filter without heating — one should be careful, as the primary practice, not to heat it to a burning heat. One should also be warned that if ants are seen to have fallen into honey or another beverage, they should be filtered out immediately and not left for three days, so the honey is not considered "pickled" (which has the law of cooked). But with actual bee honey itself, it is impossible to be careful about this in advance, since it is brought from a distant place and arrives after already being several days old among the gentiles.
takeaways: Bee honey with bee bodies in it — as the primary practice should not be heated to a burning heat; after the fact, permitted.
Honey with fallen ants should be filtered immediately, not left three days; heating to a burning heat is forbidden as the primary practice.
With imported bee honey, it is difficult to be careful in advance, since it arrives already several days old.

paragraphs: "p demin haddin yesh lehattir op tahor "y bediqat shelosha sammanim hamporashim bedibre chaza"l, mikkol maqom yesh poseqin machmirin usebira lehu dela mehanne hassammanim lebaddam lehattir haop, ki im raq tzarik sheyyihyeh lanu masoret veqabbala bezeh haop shehu min tahor. veken hamminhag pashut sheen lismok ki im raq al hammasoret. veim echad meid al op echad sheyyesh lo bo qabbala shehu tahor, somekin al debarayv im hu muchzaq beneemanut ukesherot veyirat-shamayim; veim eno muchzaq bekak, en somekin alayv; d"g deqayma lan: ed echad neeman beissurin - chayeshinan dilma lo diyyeq vetae. vetzarik sheyyaid sheraa minhag pashut bimdina achat sheokelin zeh haop, o sheshshama meadam gadol shehu keday lismok alayv, sheomer shezzeh haop okelin oto bimdina zo, veyesh lahem qabbala bo demuttar. veim amar sheshshama zeh meenash dealema mehamon haam, la samekinan al debarayv vekannizkar bapposeqim.

clarification.explanation: By Torah law, a pure fowl may be permitted by examining the three signs the Sages enumerated (such as an extra talon, a crop, a peelable gizzard). But some authorities are stricter, holding that the signs alone do not suffice, and that we must have a tradition and received knowledge from generation to generation that this particular fowl is pure — and this is indeed the practical, accepted custom: to rely only on the tradition and not on the signs alone. If someone testifies that he has a tradition that a certain fowl is pure, his testimony is relied upon only if he is known as a trustworthy, observant, God-fearing person; if he is not known as such, he is not relied upon — since although generally a single witness is believed in matters of permission and prohibition, here there is concern he may not have examined carefully and erred. He must testify that he personally saw the widespread practice in a certain country of eating that fowl, or that he heard this from a great and authoritative person; but if he heard it only from the simple masses, his testimony is not relied upon.
takeaways: Permitting a pure fowl requires a generational tradition, not merely an examination of the signs.
Testimony about a tradition is accepted only from a trustworthy, observant, God-fearing person.
Testimony heard only from the common masses, and not from a known practice or a great authority, does not suffice.

paragraphs: Im yesh op shebbeir zo matzuy ak en nohagim leakelo, ubeir acheret nohagim leakelo, sheyyesh lahem bo masoret lehetter - asur leanshe otah hair shennahagu bo issur, leekol mizzeh haop; dekevan denahagu issur baakilato, ulay nahagu mishshum gader useyag "p sheyyadeu sheyyesh leir acheret qabbala shel hetter bo; o yittaken nechlequ beqabbalatam; abal ir sheeno matzuy etzlam zeh haop, ulekak en yodeim bo - somekin al qabbala shel ir acheret shemmatzuy etzlam.

clarification.explanation: If there is a fowl found in a certain city whose residents avoid eating it, while in another city it is customarily eaten by virtue of a tradition that it is kosher — it is forbidden for the residents of the first city (who follow a practice forbidding it) to eat it, even though they know there is a tradition in the other city permitting it, since it is possible they adopted the prohibition as a voluntary safeguard, or perhaps there is a genuine dispute in the tradition. But in a city where the fowl is not found at all and they have no knowledge of it whatsoever, one may rely there on the tradition of the other city where it is known and accepted.
takeaways: If a city follows a practice forbidding a certain fowl, even knowing another city has a tradition permitting it, its residents remain forbidden.
A city with no tradition at all (the fowl is not found there) may rely on another city's tradition of permission.

paragraphs: Simane dagim meporashim battora: kol sheyyesh lo senappir veqasqaset, tahor. usenappir - hu sheshshat bo; qasqeset - hen haqqelippot haqqebuot bo. vedavqa im hem niqlapim beyad o bikli, abal im i epshar liqlapam meor haddag, la miqqere "qasqeset". vaapillu en lo ella senappir echad veqasqeset achat, muttar; ubekol maqom shennimtza muttar; ken hu daat maran za"l. veyesh omerim deen lehattir ella im ken omedet tachat lechayyayv o zenabo o senappiro. vetzarik lehorot kedaat mera"n za"l; vehammachmir kedaat yesh omerim, tabo alayv beraka. vedagim hannimtzaim irenu bagdad y" asher okelim otam, hem chamishsha minim: haechad hu hanniqra bearbe "bene", vehu meshubbach mikkullam; vehashsheni hanniqra "shibbut"; vehashshelishi hanniqra "abu sevivyp"; veharebii hanniqra "bez"; vehachamishi hanniqra "g'tn". vezeh hammin hanniqra "shibbut", hu hannizkar baggemara deqiddushin, resh pereq sheni (dap m.): raba melach shibbuta, vehu qoleyas haaspanin hannizkar bemasseket shabbat, dap qmh: .

clarification.explanation: The signs of fish are explicit in the Torah: anything with a "fin" (by which it swims) and "scales" (fixed shells on it) is pure — provided the scales can be peeled off by hand or with an implement, but if they cannot be peeled from the fish's skin, they are not considered "scales." And even if it has only one fin and one scale — it is permitted, and wherever the scale is found on it — it is permitted; so is Maran's view. Some say it is permitted only if the scale is under its jaw, tail, or fin; the ruling should follow Maran, though one who is stringent following the "some say" view is blessed. The fish eaten in Baghdad are five kinds: "bini" (the finest of all), "shabbut," "abu suwayf," "biz," and "jattan"; and the "shabbut" is the one mentioned in the Gemara (Kiddushin — "Rava salted shabbuta"), and it is the "kulyas ha'ispanin" mentioned in tractate Shabbat.
takeaways: A pure fish has a fin and a scale peelable by hand or implement; even one fin and one scale, wherever located, suffices to permit it (following Maran).
Some require the scale to be under the jaw, tail, or fin; the ruling follows Maran, though the stringent view is blessed.
